notes.front: What is a replica?
notes.back: A copy of a Pod; several identical replicas give availability, scalability and fault tolerance.
notes.explanation: Running more instances of an application means running more Pods, one per instance; this is called replication.
notes.example: Three replicas of a web server spread over nodes: if one node fails, two copies keep serving.

notes.front: What is a ReplicaSet?
notes.back: An object that keeps a stable set of identical replica Pods running at any given time.
notes.explanation: Using a selector, a replica count and a Pod template, it creates or deletes Pods as needed to reach the desired number.
notes.example: A ReplicaSet set to 3: delete one of its Pods and it immediately makes a new one from its template.

notes.front: What is a Deployment?
notes.back: An object that manages a replicated, usually stateless, application by managing ReplicaSets, which in turn run the Pods.
notes.explanation: You declare the desired state and the Deployment controller moves the actual state to it at a controlled rate; it is the most common way to run an application. Stateless means it keeps no data of its own between requests, so any copy can serve any user.
notes.example: Declare “3 copies of shop:v2”: the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually replaces the v1 Pods.

image.alt: Ownership during a rolling update of a Deployment with 4 desired Pods. The Deployment owns two ReplicaSets: the old one (revision 1, image v1) scaling down and the new one (revision 2, image v2) scaling up. Each ReplicaSet owns its own Pods. A note gives the default bounds: maxUnavailable 25% and maxSurge 25%, so with 4 desired Pods at least 3 stay available and at most 5 exist at once.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from Kubernetes documentation, “Deployments”

notes.front: What are a Deployment's two update strategies?
notes.back: RollingUpdate (the default) replaces Pods gradually; Recreate kills all existing Pods before creating new ones.
notes.explanation: The choice is set in .spec.strategy.type; Recreate means a gap in service but guarantees old Pods are gone before new ones start.
notes.example: A web front end usually rolls; an app that must never run two versions at once can use Recreate.

notes.front: What do maxUnavailable and maxSurge control?
notes.back: During a rolling update: how many Pods may be unavailable below, and how many extra may exist above, the desired count.
notes.explanation: Each can be a number or a percentage of desired Pods; they cannot both be 0.
notes.example: With 4 desired Pods and the defaults, at least 3 stay available and at most 5 exist at any moment.

notes.front: What does rolling back a Deployment do?
notes.back: Returns it to an earlier revision, whose Pod template is kept in one of its old ReplicaSets.
notes.explanation: A new revision is created only when the Deployment's Pod template changes; each rollback also updates the revision.
notes.example: Version 2 crash-loops after rollout, so you roll back to revision 1 and the old image returns.

notes.front: What does a Deployment's revisionHistoryLimit set?
notes.back: How many old ReplicaSets the Deployment keeps so that you can roll back to them.
notes.explanation: Each revision's configuration lives in its ReplicaSet, so a deleted old ReplicaSet means that revision can no longer be restored.
notes.example: Like keeping the last few versions of a document: older drafts beyond the limit are thrown away for good.

notes.front: What is a ReplicationController?
notes.back: A legacy API that keeps a set number of Pod replicas running, superseded by Deployment and ReplicaSet.
notes.explanation: The documentation now recommends a Deployment that configures a ReplicaSet for replication.
notes.example: Like an old version of a form: it still works, but new applications use the replacement.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What is a StatefulSet?
notes.back: A workload object for data-keeping apps: each Pod gets a fixed name (web-0, web-1…), keeps its own storage when replaced, and starts in order.
notes.explanation: Unlike a Deployment's interchangeable Pods, each StatefulSet Pod keeps its identity across rescheduling, so it can be matched to its own persistent storage.
notes.example: A three-member database cluster in which each member must keep its own name and its own data.

notes.front: What is a StatefulSet Pod's ordinal index?
notes.back: A unique integer, from 0 to N−1 for N replicas, that forms part of the Pod's name and identity.
notes.explanation: Each Pod's hostname is the StatefulSet's name plus its ordinal, and the controller also adds a label holding the index.
notes.example: A StatefulSet called web with 3 replicas runs Pods web-0, web-1 and web-2.

notes.front: What is a DaemonSet?
notes.back: An object that makes all (or some) nodes each run a copy of a Pod; new nodes get one, removed nodes' copies are cleaned up.
notes.explanation: It suits helpers that must run on each machine, such as a log collector or a monitoring agent that must run on every node.
notes.example: A log collector that reads log files on each machine runs as a DaemonSet, one Pod per node.

notes.front: What is a Job?
notes.back: An object that creates Pods and keeps retrying until a specified number of them complete successfully.
notes.explanation: It represents a one-off task that runs to completion and then stops; deleting the Job cleans up its Pods.
notes.example: A one-off data import that must finish once, even if a node reboots halfway through.

notes.front: What is a CronJob?
notes.back: An object that starts a Job on a repeating timetable of five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, weekday), in Unix cron style.
notes.explanation: cron is the classic Unix scheduler; one CronJob is like one line of its timetable file (a crontab). Typical uses are backups and report generation.
notes.example: A CronJob with schedule 0 3 * * 1 starts a backup Job every Monday at 03:00.

notes.front: What is a ConfigMap?
notes.back: An API object that stores non-confidential configuration data as key-value pairs for Pods to use.
notes.explanation: It keeps environment-specific settings out of the container image, making applications portable; it offers no secrecy or encryption.
notes.example: The same image reads DATABASE_HOST: set to localhost on a laptop, and to the cluster's database address in the cloud.

notes.front: What is a Secret?
notes.back: An object that holds a small amount of sensitive data, such as a password, a token or a key.
notes.explanation: It keeps confidential data out of Pod specifications and container images; it is like a ConfigMap but intended for confidential data.
notes.example: A database password reaches a Pod as an environment variable from a Secret instead of being baked into the image.

notes.front: What are blue-green deployment and canary deployment?
notes.back: Blue-green: two environments, with all production traffic switched to the updated one at once. Canary: live traffic moved to the new version gradually.
notes.explanation: Both reduce the risk of a release; canary lets you test in production on a small share of traffic and quickly roll back.
notes.example: Canary: 1%, then 10%, then 25% of traffic to v2. Blue-green: test green, then flip all traffic from blue to green.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary, “Blue Green Deployment” and “Canary Deployment”

notes.front: Kubernetes creates containers for the new version of an app and removes the old ones at a controlled rate, and can undo this. Which capability is this?
notes.back: Automated rollouts and rollbacks.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes can create new containers, remove old ones and move their resources across.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: What is a workload in Kubernetes?
notes.back: An application running on Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: Built-in workload APIs create and manage Pods for you, so you rarely create Pods directly, even single ones.
notes.example: A shop made of a web server and a database is one workload; each part runs under its own workload object.

notes.front: A web shop runs on Kubernetes as a web server plus a database. In Kubernetes terms, what is the shop as a whole?
notes.back: One workload; its database might run in a StatefulSet and its web server in a Deployment.
notes.explanation: A workload is an application running on Kubernetes; each of its parts is managed by a workload object suited to it.

notes.front: Besides long-running services, Kubernetes can run tasks that finish (batch jobs), replacing containers that fail. Which capability is this?
notes.back: Batch execution.
notes.explanation: Work that runs to completion is managed alongside always-on services.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: Should you directly manage ReplicaSets that a Deployment owns?
notes.back: No. Manage the Deployment; it creates, scales and retires its ReplicaSets.
notes.explanation: The documentation's note on Deployments says not to manage ReplicaSets owned by a Deployment.

notes.front: Kubernetes stores passwords and keys, and lets you update application configuration without rebuilding container images. Which capability is this?
notes.back: Its “secret and configuration management”.
notes.explanation: Sensitive values are not exposed in your stack configuration.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: When does the documentation suggest using a ReplicaSet directly instead of a Deployment?
notes.back: Only if you need custom update orchestration or no updates at all.
notes.explanation: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and adds declarative updates to Pods, so it is the recommended choice.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “ReplicaSet”, “When to use a ReplicaSet”

notes.front: What change, and only what change, triggers a Deployment rollout?
notes.back: A change to the Deployment's Pod template (.spec.template), such as a new image or labels.
notes.explanation: Other updates, such as scaling the Deployment, do not trigger a rollout or create a revision.

notes.front: If a Deployment's .spec.replicas is not set, how many Pods does it run?
notes.explanation: If an autoscaler manages the Deployment's scaling, leave .spec.replicas unset and let the control plane manage it.

notes.front: A Deployment's default .spec.strategy.type is {{c1::RollingUpdate}}.
notes.explanation: The only other value is Recreate.

notes.front: What are the default values of maxUnavailable and maxSurge?
notes.back: 25% each.
notes.explanation: So by default at least 75% of the desired Pods are up, and at most 125% exist, during an update.

notes.front: When maxUnavailable and maxSurge are percentages, which way is each rounded to a whole number of Pods?
notes.back: maxUnavailable rounds down; maxSurge rounds up.
notes.explanation: For example, 25% of 10 desired Pods allows 2 unavailable (2.5 rounded down) and 3 extra (rounded up).

notes.front: How many old ReplicaSets does a Deployment keep for rollback by default?
notes.explanation: The rest are garbage-collected; the right number depends on how often and how stably you deploy.

notes.front: Which restartPolicy may the Pods of a Deployment use?
notes.back: Only Always.
notes.explanation: A Deployment keeps applications running continuously, so Always is the only allowed value.

notes.front: Which restartPolicy values may a Job's Pod template use?
notes.back: Only Never or OnFailure.
notes.explanation: Jobs are batch tasks that end; Always would restart a container after any exit, even a successful one.

notes.front: By default, how many retries does a Job allow before it is marked failed?
notes.back: 6 (.spec.backoffLimit).
notes.explanation: Each Pod failure counts toward the limit; you can set your own number of retries.

notes.front: In what order does a StatefulSet with N replicas create its Pods, and in what order does it delete them?
notes.back: Creates them one by one from 0 to N−1; deletes them in reverse, from N−1 to 0.
notes.explanation: Before a scaling operation is applied to a Pod, all of its predecessors must be Running and Ready.

notes.front: When you delete or scale down a StatefulSet, is the storage attached to its Pods deleted? (Storage is covered in the Storage topic.)
notes.back: No; it is kept, for data safety.
notes.explanation: The documentation values data safety over an automatic purge, so the storage must be removed manually.

notes.front: What pattern gives each StatefulSet Pod its hostname?
notes.back: The StatefulSet's name, a hyphen, then the Pod's ordinal.
notes.explanation: Because the name comes from the ordinal, it stays the same when the Pod is replaced.

notes.front: What typical uses does the documentation give for a DaemonSet?
notes.back: Running a cluster storage daemon (a background program), a log collection daemon, or a node monitoring daemon on every node.
notes.explanation: Each DaemonSet Pod plays a role like a system daemon on a classic Unix server.

notes.front: In a CronJob schedule, which field comes last, and what does 0 mean in it?
notes.back: Day of the week (0–6); 0 means Sunday.
notes.explanation: The five fields are minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week.

notes.front: What is the maximum length of a CronJob's name, and why?
notes.back: 52 characters, because the controller appends 11 characters and Job names may not exceed 63.
notes.explanation: The CronJob's name forms part of the names of the Jobs and Pods it creates.

notes.front: Why should the Jobs a CronJob runs be idempotent?
notes.back: Scheduling is approximate: occasionally two Jobs, or none, may be created for one scheduled time.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes tries to avoid this but does not completely prevent it.

notes.front: What is the maximum size of the data in a ConfigMap?
notes.back: 1 MiB.
notes.explanation: A ConfigMap is not meant for large chunks of data; for bigger settings, use a separate database or file service.

notes.front: Must a Pod and the ConfigMap it refers to be in the same namespace?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: A Pod spec that refers to a ConfigMap configures its containers from that ConfigMap's data.

notes.front: If a Pod consumes a ConfigMap as environment variables and the ConfigMap changes, does the Pod see the new values?
notes.back: No; environment variables are not updated automatically, so the Pod must be restarted.
notes.explanation: ConfigMaps mounted as files, by contrast, are updated automatically after a delay.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “ConfigMaps”, “Mounted ConfigMaps are updated automatically”

notes.front: By default, how are Secrets stored in etcd?
notes.back: Unencrypted: the values are only base64-encoded, a reversible text format anyone can decode.
notes.explanation: Anyone with API access or etcd access can read them, so turn on encryption at rest (encrypting the data where it is stored) and restrict access.

notes.front: What is the size limit of an individual Secret?
notes.back: 1 MiB.
notes.explanation: The limit discourages very large Secrets that could exhaust API server and kubelet memory.

notes.front: Who can indirectly read every Secret in a namespace, even without direct Secret access?
notes.back: Anyone authorised to create a Pod in that namespace, including through something like a Deployment.
notes.explanation: A Pod can mount or reference any Secret in its namespace, so Pod-creation rights imply Secret access.

notes.front: In canary deployment, where does the name “canary” come from?
notes.back: Canaries once taken into coal mines: if the bird died, miners knew to get out.
notes.explanation: Likewise, if the updated code goes wrong, live traffic is “evacuated” back to the original version.

notes.front: A stateless web front end (keeping no data of its own between requests) must run 5 interchangeable copies and be updated without downtime. Which workload resource fits?
notes.back: A Deployment.
notes.explanation: Deployments suit stateless applications whose Pods are interchangeable and replaceable.

notes.front: A replicated database needs each member to keep a stable name and its own storage across restarts. Which workload resource fits?
notes.back: A StatefulSet.
notes.explanation: StatefulSets give each Pod a sticky identity, so replacements reconnect to the same storage.

notes.front: A monitoring agent must run exactly one copy on every node, including nodes added later. Which workload resource fits?
notes.back: A DaemonSet.
notes.explanation: A DaemonSet adds its Pod to each new node automatically.

notes.front: A data migration must run once to successful completion and then stop. Which workload resource fits?
notes.back: A Job.
notes.explanation: A Job retries its Pods until the required number complete successfully, then it is complete.

notes.front: A report must be generated every night at 02:00. Which workload resource fits?
notes.back: A CronJob.
notes.explanation: A CronJob creates a Job for each scheduled run; a plain Job would run only once.

notes.front: What does the CronJob schedule 0 3 * * 1 mean?
notes.back: Every Monday at 03:00.
notes.explanation: The fields are minute (0), hour (3), day of month (*), month (*) and day of week (1, Monday).

notes.front: Someone deletes one of the 3 Pods a ReplicaSet manages. What does the ReplicaSet do?
notes.back: Creates a new Pod from its template to get back to 3.
notes.explanation: A ReplicaSet creates and deletes Pods as needed to reach its desired number.

notes.front: You scale a Deployment from 3 to 5 replicas. Does this create a new revision you could roll back to?
notes.back: No. Only a change to the Pod template triggers a rollout and a new revision.
notes.explanation: Scaling changes the replica count, not the template, so the revision history is unchanged.

notes.front: A Deployment with 10 replicas rolls out using the default bounds. What is the least number available, and the most that can exist?
notes.back: At least 8 available; at most 13 in total.
notes.explanation: 25% of 10 is 2.5: maxUnavailable rounds down to 2, maxSurge rounds up to 3.

notes.front: A Deployment has revisionHistoryLimit set to 0. A new rollout goes badly. Can you roll it back?
notes.back: No; all old ReplicaSets are cleaned up, so there is no history to roll back to.
notes.explanation: Each revision's configuration lives only in its ReplicaSet.

notes.front: A Deployment uses the Recreate strategy. During an upgrade, are old and new Pods ever running together?
notes.back: No. All old Pods are terminated, and their removal awaited, before any new Pod is created.
notes.explanation: That guarantee costs a period with no Pods serving; RollingUpdate avoids the gap but runs both versions briefly.

notes.front: A Job's Pod template sets restartPolicy: Always. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. A Job allows only Never or OnFailure.
notes.explanation: Always would keep restarting a container that has already finished its task.

notes.front: A Job's Pod keeps failing and you set no backoffLimit. How many retries happen before the Job is marked failed?
notes.explanation: The default .spec.backoffLimit is 6 (unless a per-index backoff limit is set).

notes.front: A StatefulSet named db runs 3 replicas and is scaled down to 1. Which Pod is terminated first?
notes.back: db-2.
notes.explanation: StatefulSet Pods are named db-0 to db-2 and are removed in reverse ordinal order.

notes.front: A new node joins a cluster that runs a log-collecting DaemonSet. What happens?
notes.back: The DaemonSet adds its Pod to the new node automatically.
notes.explanation: As nodes are added, DaemonSet Pods are added to them; as nodes leave, those Pods are garbage-collected.

notes.front: An application needs an API token for a payment provider. ConfigMap or Secret?
notes.back: A Secret.
notes.explanation: Secrets are for confidential data; a ConfigMap provides no secrecy or encryption.

notes.front: An application reads a LOG_LEVEL setting that differs between test and production. ConfigMap or Secret?
notes.back: A ConfigMap.
notes.explanation: It is non-confidential, environment-specific configuration, exactly what a ConfigMap is for.

notes.front: A colleague says a Secret is safe because its value looks scrambled. Is it encrypted?
notes.back: No. It is only base64-encoded, and stored unencrypted in etcd unless encryption at rest is enabled.
notes.explanation: Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse; protection comes from encryption at rest and tight access control.

notes.front: A team sends 5% of live traffic to a new version, watches for errors, then raises the share step by step. Which strategy is this?
notes.back: Canary deployment.
notes.explanation: Blue-green would switch all production traffic from one environment to the other at once.

notes.front: A shop keeps two full environments, tests the idle one, then switches all production traffic to it at once. Which strategy is this?
notes.back: Blue-green deployment.
notes.explanation: Canary would move traffic gradually rather than all at once.

notes.front: An old tutorial uses a ReplicationController. What should a new setup use instead?
notes.back: A Deployment, which configures a ReplicaSet.
notes.explanation: ReplicationController has been superseded by the Deployment and ReplicaSet APIs.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: How do the Pods of a Deployment differ from the Pods of a StatefulSet?
notes.back: Deployment Pods are interchangeable; each StatefulSet Pod keeps a sticky identity, name and storage.
notes.explanation: If an application needs no stable identifiers or ordering, the documentation points to a Deployment instead.

notes.front: What does a Deployment add on top of a ReplicaSet?
notes.back: Declarative updates: rolling out new versions through new ReplicaSets, and rolling back.
notes.explanation: A ReplicaSet only keeps a set number of identical Pods running.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “ReplicaSet”, “When to use a ReplicaSet”

notes.front: How does a Job differ from a CronJob?
notes.back: A Job is a one-off task run to completion; a CronJob creates such Jobs repeatedly on a schedule.
notes.explanation: Use a Job for “run this once”, a CronJob for “run this every night”.

notes.front: How does a DaemonSet decide how many Pods to run, compared with a Deployment?
notes.back: DaemonSet: one per eligible node, following the nodes. Deployment: a replica count you set, placed on any nodes.
notes.explanation: Add a node and a DaemonSet grows; a Deployment's count stays the same.

notes.front: What is the main difference in purpose between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
notes.back: A ConfigMap is for non-confidential data; a Secret is for confidential data such as passwords and keys.
notes.explanation: Both are key-value objects Pods can use; neither is encrypted in etcd by default.

notes.front: What does RollingUpdate trade off against Recreate?
notes.back: RollingUpdate avoids downtime but briefly runs old and new versions together; Recreate avoids mixing but has downtime.
notes.explanation: Recreate terminates every old Pod before creating new ones.
